1	# Independent Analysis of AI Models and API Providers -- Artificial Analysis, April 2026
     2	
     3	## Source
     4	
     5	- URL: https://artificialanalysis.ai/
     6	- Captured: April 10, 2026
     7	
     8	Artificial Analysis is an independent platform that benchmarks large language models across intelligence, speed, and pricing. The data below reflects the latest evaluations published in April 2026, covering both proprietary and open-weight models from major AI labs worldwide.
     9	
    10	## Intelligence Index: Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview and GPT-5.4 Share the Lead at 57
    11	
    12	The Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index is a composite score aggregating performance across a wide range of reasoning, knowledge, and instruction-following benchmarks. Higher scores indicate stronger overall capability.
    13	
    14	As of April 2026, two models share the top position:
    15	
    16	| Rank | Model | Provider | Intelligence Index |
    17	|------|-------|----------|--------------------|
    18	| 1 | Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview | Google | 57 |
    19	| 2 | GPT-5.4 (xhigh) | OpenAI | 57 |
    20	| 3 | Claude Opus 4.6 (max) | Anthropic | 53 |
    21	| 4 | Muse Spark | Meta | 52 |
    22	| 5 | Claude Sonnet 4.6 (max) | Anthropic | 52 |
    23	| 6 | GLM-5.1 | Z AI | 51 |
    24	| 7 | Grok 4.20 0309 v2 | xAI | 49 |
    25	| 8 | Gemini 3 Flash | Google | 46 |
    26	| 9 | DeepSeek V3.2 | DeepSeek | 42 |
    27	| 10 | NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Super | NVIDIA | 36 |
    28	| 11 | gpt-oss-120B (high) | OpenAI | 33 |
    29	
    30	Google and OpenAI are neck-and-neck at the frontier. Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6 trails by 4 points, while Meta's newly released Muse Spark enters at a strong 52. Open-weight models such as GLM-5.1 and Grok 4.20 occupy the mid-tier, demonstrating that the gap between proprietary and open-weight models continues to narrow.
    31	
    32	![Intelligence Index ranking of top AI models, April 2026](./assets/chart_intelligence_index_ranking.jpg)
    33	
    34	## Output Speed: Open-Weight Models Dominate Throughput
    35	
    36	Inference speed, measured in output tokens per second, is critical for latency-sensitive applications. The leaderboard shows a striking pattern: open-weight and smaller models generate tokens far faster than frontier proprietary models.
    37	
    38	| Rank | Model | Output Tokens/s |
    39	|------|-------|-----------------|
    40	| 1 | gpt-oss-120B (high) | 218 |
    41	| 2 | Grok 4.20 0309 v2 | 188 |
    42	| 3 | NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Super | 172 |
    43	| 4 | Gemini 3 Flash | 153 |
    44	| 5 | Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview | 118 |
    45	| 6 | GPT-5.4 (xhigh) | 83 |
    46	| 7 | GLM-5.1 | 64 |
    47	| 8 | Claude Sonnet 4.6 (max) | 63 |
    48	| 9 | Claude Opus 4.6 (max) | 49 |
    49	| 10 | DeepSeek V3.2 | 46 |
    50	
    51	The fastest model, gpt-oss-120B (high), outputs 218 tokens per second -- more than 4x the speed of Claude Opus 4.6 and nearly 5x that of DeepSeek V3.2. This highlights the trade-off between raw intelligence and throughput: the two intelligence leaders (Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview and GPT-5.4) sit in the middle of the speed table at 118 and 83 tokens/s respectively.
    52	
    53	![Output speed ranking by tokens per second](./assets/chart_output_speed_ranking.jpg)
    54	
    55	## Pricing: A 33x Gap Between Cheapest and Most Expensive
    56	
    57	API pricing per million tokens varies enormously across models, reflecting differences in compute requirements, margin strategies, and competitive positioning.
    58	
    59	| Rank | Model | USD per 1M Tokens |
    60	|------|-------|--------------------|
    61	| 1 | gpt-oss-120B (high) | $0.30 |
    62	| 2 | DeepSeek V3.2 | $0.30 |
    63	| 3 | NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Super | $0.40 |
    64	| 4 | Gemini 3 Flash | $1.10 |
    65	| 5 | GLM-5.1 | $2.10 |
    66	| 6 | Grok 4.20 0309 v2 | $3.00 |
    67	| 7 | Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview | $4.50 |
    68	| 8 | GPT-5.4 (xhigh) | $5.60 |
    69	| 9 | Claude Sonnet 4.6 (max) | $6.00 |
    70	| 10 | Claude Opus 4.6 (max) | $10.00 |
    71	
    72	The cheapest options -- gpt-oss-120B and DeepSeek V3.2 at $0.30 per million tokens -- are over 33x less expensive than Claude Opus 4.6 at $10.00. For budget-sensitive workloads, this price differential is a decisive factor. Notably, Gemini 3 Flash offers a compelling mid-range value at $1.10, pairing solid speed (153 tokens/s) with reasonable intelligence (46).
    73	
    74	![Price per million tokens comparison across models](./assets/chart_price_per_million_tokens.jpg)
    75	
    76	## The Intelligence-Throughput Frontier: Finding the "Most Attractive Quadrant"
    77	
    78	A scatter plot of Intelligence Index versus output tokens consumed during evaluation reveals which models occupy the "most attractive quadrant" -- high intelligence with efficient token usage. Models that achieve high scores while consuming fewer tokens represent better engineering and more efficient architectures.
    79	
    80	Key observations from the scatter plot:
    81	
    82	- Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview and DeepSeek V3.2 cluster in the upper region, indicating strong intelligence scores.
    83	- Grok 4.20 0309 v2 and several Google models sit in the middle-right region, balancing intelligence and token efficiency.
    84	- Llama 4 Maverick occupies the low-intelligence, low-token region, suggesting it is neither efficient nor highly capable.
    85	- MiMo-V2-Pro appears in the upper-right corner, showing very high intelligence but with substantial token usage.
    86	
    87	![Scatter plot of intelligence index vs output tokens, highlighting the most attractive quadrant](./assets/chart_intelligence_vs_output_tokens.jpg)
    88	
    89	## Proprietary vs. Open-Weight Models
    90	
    91	The April 2026 landscape shows proprietary models still leading on raw intelligence, but the margin is thin. GLM-5.1, an open-weight model from Z AI, scores 51 -- just 6 points behind the co-leaders. Meanwhile, open-weight models like gpt-oss-120B dominate on speed and price. The intelligence leaderboard includes models from at least 8 distinct organizations across the US, China, and Europe, reflecting a genuinely global competition.
    92	
    93	| Metric | Proprietary Leader | Score | Open-Weight Leader | Score |
    94	|--------|--------------------|-------|--------------------|-------|
    95	| Intelligence | Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview | 57 | GLM-5.1 | 51 |
    96	| Speed (tokens/s) | Gemini 3 Flash | 153 | gpt-oss-120B (high) | 218 |
    97	| Price ($/1M tokens) | Gemini 3 Flash | $1.10 | gpt-oss-120B (high) | $0.30 |
    98	
    99	## Key Findings
   100	
   101	- **Two-way tie at the top**: Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview and GPT-5.4 (xhigh) both score 57 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, making them the co-leaders as of April 2026.
   102	- **Speed and intelligence are inversely correlated**: The fastest model (gpt-oss-120B at 218 tokens/s) scores only 33 on intelligence, while the smartest models operate at 49-118 tokens/s.
   103	- **Massive pricing spread**: A 33x cost gap separates the cheapest ($0.30/1M tokens for gpt-oss-120B and DeepSeek V3.2) from the most expensive ($10.00/1M tokens for Claude Opus 4.6).
   104	- **Open-weight models are closing the gap**: GLM-5.1 at 51 intelligence is within 10% of the proprietary leaders, while also being significantly cheaper at $2.10/1M tokens.
   105	- **No single model wins on all three axes**: Choosing a model requires explicit trade-offs among intelligence, speed, and cost depending on the use case.

Use when (1) the task is about PowerPoint or `.pptx`; (2) layouts, placeholders, notes, charts, comments, or template fidelity matter; (3) the deck must render cleanly after edits."

     9	---
    10	
    11	## When to Use
    12	
    13	Use when the main artifact is a Microsoft PowerPoint presentation or `.pptx` deck, especially when layouts, templates, placeholders, notes, comments, charts, extraction, editing, or final visual quality matter.
    14	
    15	## Core Rules
    16	
    17	### 1. Choose the workflow before touching the deck
    18	
    19	- Reading text, editing an existing deck, rebuilding from a template, and creating from scratch are different jobs with different failure modes.
    20	- For text extraction or inspection, read the deck before editing it.
    21	- Text extraction plus thumbnail-style visual inspection is safer than editing from shape assumptions alone.
    22	- For template-driven work, inventory the deck before replacing content.
    23	- For deep edits, remember a `.pptx` file is OOXML with separate parts for slides, layouts, masters, media, notes, and comments.
    24	- If a template exists, template fidelity beats generic slide-design instincts.
    25	- Reusing or duplicating a good existing slide is often safer than rebuilding it and hoping the theme still matches.
    26	
    27	### 2. Inventory the deck before replacing content
    28	
    29	- Count the reusable layouts, real placeholders, notes, comments, media, and recurring typography or color patterns first.
    30	- Placeholder indexes and layout indexes are not portable assumptions.
    31	- Inspect the actual slide or template before targeting title, body, chart, or image shapes.
    32	- Speaker notes, comments, and linked assets can live outside the visible slide surface.
    33	- A missing or wrong placeholder target can silently land content in the wrong box or wrong layer.
    34	- Master and layout settings can override local slide edits, so the visible problem is not always on the slide you are editing.
    35	
    36	### 3. Match content to the actual placeholders
    37	
    38	- Count the actual content pieces before choosing a layout.
    39	- Pick layouts based on the real number of ideas, columns, images, or charts the slide needs.
    40	- Do not force two ideas into a three-column slide or cram dense text under a chart.
    41	- Category counts and data series lengths must match or charts will break in ugly ways.
    42	- Explicit sizing beats wishful thinking: text boxes, images, and charts need real space, not "it should fit".
    43	- Do not choose a layout with more placeholders than the content can meaningfully fill.
    44	- Quote layouts are for real quotes, and image-led layouts are for slides that actually have images.
    45	- For chart-, table-, or image-heavy slides, full-slide or two-column layouts are usually safer than stacking dense text above the visual.
    46	
    47	### 4. Preserve the deck's visual language
    48	
    49	- Theme, master, and layout files usually decide fonts, colors, and hierarchy more than any one slide does.
    50	- Start from the deck's actual theme, fonts, spacing, and aspect ratio instead of improvising a new style.
    51	- Reuse the deck's own alignment and spacing system instead of inventing a second visual language.
    52	- Use common fonts for portability and strong contrast for readability.
    53	- Preserve the template's visual logic first; originality matters less than not breaking the deck's existing language.
    54	- Combining slides from multiple sources requires normalizing themes, masters, and alignment afterward.
    55	
    56	### 5. Run content QA and visual QA separately
    57	
    58	- Text overflow, bad alignment, clipped shapes, weak contrast, and placeholder leftovers are normal first-pass failures.
    59	- Run both content QA and visual QA; missing text and broken layout are different failure classes.
    60	- Render or inspect the actual deck output before delivery when layout matters.
    61	- Search for leftover template junk, sample labels, and placeholder text before calling the deck finished.
    62	- Check notes, comments, labels, legends, and chart/table semantics separately from the visual pass.
    63	- A deck can pass text extraction and still fail on overlap, clipping, wrong theme inheritance, or broken notes.
    64	- Thumbnail grids and rendered slides usually reveal layout bugs faster than code or text inspection.
    65	- Assume the first render is wrong and do at least one fix-and-verify cycle before calling the deck finished.
    66	- Re-check affected slides after each fix because one spacing change often creates another issue.
    67	
    68	### 6. Keep decks portable and review-safe
    69	
    70	- Template masters can override direct edits in surprising ways.
    71	- Complex effects may degrade across PowerPoint, LibreOffice, and conversion pipelines, so keep important content robust without them.
    72	- Image sizing, font substitution, and placeholder mismatch are common reasons a deck looks good in code and bad on screen.
    73	- Notes, comments, linked media, and merged decks can stay broken even when the visible slide looks fine.
    74	
    75	## Common Traps
    76	
    77	- Placeholder text and sample charts often survive template reuse if not explicitly replaced.
    78	- Directly editing one slide can fail if the real issue lives in the master or layout.
    79	- Charts, icons, and text boxes need enough space; near-collisions are usually visible only after rendering.
    80	- Layout indexes vary by template, so built-in assumptions from one deck often break in another.
    81	- A missing placeholder or wrong shape target can silently put content in the wrong place.
    82	- Counting the text ideas after choosing the layout usually leads to empty placeholders, weak hierarchy, or leftover template junk.
    83	- Font substitution can move line breaks and wreck careful spacing.
    84	- Speaker notes, comments, and linked media can stay broken even when the visible slide looks fine.
    85	- A deck can pass text inspection and still fail visually because of overlap, contrast, or edge clipping.
    86	- Editing from one slide alone can miss the real source of truth in the theme, master, or layout definitions.
    87	- Choosing a quote, comparison, or multi-column layout without matching content usually makes the deck look templated rather than intentional.
    88	- Combining or duplicating slides without checking masters and themes can create subtle inconsistency slide by slide.
    89	- Aspect-ratio mismatches like `16:9` versus `4:3` can shift every placement decision even when each slide looks locally reasonable.
    90

from pptx import Presentation
from pptx.util import Inches, Pt
from pptx.enum.text import PP_ALIGN, MSO_ANCHOR
from pptx.dml.color import RGBColor
from pptx.enum.shapes import MSO_SHAPE

# Create presentation 16:9
prs = Presentation()
prs.slide_width = Inches(13.333)
prs.slide_height = Inches(7.5)

# Color palette
COLOR_BG = RGBColor(18, 24, 38)          # dark navy background
COLOR_ACCENT = RGBColor(0, 180, 216)     # teal accent
COLOR_TEXT = RGBColor(240, 240, 240)     # off-white
COLOR_TEXT_DIM = RGBColor(180, 190, 210) # dimmed text
COLOR_BAR_TOP = RGBColor(0, 180, 216)    # teal
COLOR_BAR_MID = RGBColor(100, 140, 220)  # blue-purple
COLOR_BAR_LOW = RGBColor(180, 100, 180)  # purple

# Helper: add title + subtitle text box
def add_title_slide(prs, title, subtitle):
    blank = prs.slide_layouts[6]  # blank
    slide = prs.slides.add_slide(blank)
    # Background
    background = slide.shapes.add_shape(MSO_SHAPE.RECTANGLE, 0, 0, prs.slide_width, prs.slide_height)
    background.fill.solid()
    background.fill.fore_color.rgb = COLOR_BG
    background.line.fill.background()
    # Send to back
    spTree = slide.shapes._spTree
    sp = background._element
    spTree.remove(sp)
    spTree.insert(2, sp)
    # Accent bar
    bar = slide.shapes.add_shape(MSO_SHAPE.RECTANGLE, Inches(0.8), Inches(3.0), Inches(0.15), Inches(1.5))
    bar.fill.solid()
    bar.fill.fore_color.rgb = COLOR_ACCENT
    bar.line.fill.background()
    # Title
    title_box = slide.shapes.add_textbox(Inches(1.1), Inches(2.8), Inches(11), Inches(1.8))
    tf = title_box.text_frame
    tf.word_wrap = True
    p = tf.paragraphs[0]
    p.text = title
    p.font.size = Pt(40)
    p.font.bold = True
    p.font.color.rgb = COLOR_TEXT
    p.font.name = "Calibri"
    # Subtitle
    sub_box = slide.shapes.add_textbox(Inches(1.1), Inches(4.7), Inches(11), Inches(0.8))
    tf2 = sub_box.text_frame
    tf2.word_wrap = True
    p2 = tf2.paragraphs[0]
    p2.text = subtitle
    p2.font.size = Pt(20)
    p2.font.color.rgb = COLOR_TEXT_DIM
    p2.font.name = "Calibri"
    return slide

# Helper: add section header slide
def add_section_slide(prs, title, subtitle=""):
    blank = prs.slide_layouts[6]
    slide = prs.slides.add_slide(blank)
    background = slide.shapes.add_shape(MSO_SHAPE.RECTANGLE, 0, 0, prs.slide_width, prs.slide_height)
    background.fill.solid()
    background.fill.fore_color.rgb = COLOR_BG
    background.line.fill.background()
    spTree = slide.shapes._spTree
    sp = background._element
    spTree.remove(sp)
    spTree.insert(2, sp)
    # Top accent bar
    bar = slide.shapes.add_shape(MSO_SHAPE.RECTANGLE, 0, 0, prs.slide_width, Inches(0.08))
    bar.fill.solid()
    bar.fill.fore_color.rgb = COLOR_ACCENT
    bar.line.fill.background()
    # Title
    title_box = slide.shapes.add_textbox(Inches(0.8), Inches(2.6), Inches(11.5), Inches(1.2))
    tf = title_box.text_frame
    tf.word_wrap = True
    p = tf.paragraphs[0]
    p.text = title
    p.font.size = Pt(36)
    p.font.bold = True
    p.font.color.rgb = COLOR_TEXT
    p.font.name = "Calibri"
    if subtitle:
        p2 = tf.add_paragraph()
        p2.text = subtitle
        p2.font.size = Pt(20)
        p2.font.color.rgb = COLOR_TEXT_DIM
        p2.font.name = "Calibri"
        p2.space_before = Pt(12)
    return slide

# Helper: content slide with title area
def add_content_slide(prs, title):
    blank = prs.slide_layouts[6]
    slide = prs.slides.add_slide(blank)
    background = slide.shapes.add_shape(MSO_SHAPE.RECTANGLE, 0, 0, prs.slide_width, prs.slide_height)
    background.fill.solid()
    background.fill.fore_color.rgb = COLOR_BG
    background.line.fill.background()
    spTree = slide.shapes._spTree
    sp = background._element
    spTree.remove(sp)
    spTree.insert(2, sp)
    # Top accent bar
    bar = slide.shapes.add_shape(MSO_SHAPE.RECTANGLE, 0, 0, prs.slide_width, Inches(0.06))
    bar.fill.solid()
    bar.fill.fore_color.rgb = COLOR_ACCENT
    bar.line.fill.background()
    # Title
    title_box = slide.shapes.add_textbox(Inches(0.6), Inches(0.35), Inches(12), Inches(0.7))
    tf = title_box.text_frame
    p = tf.paragraphs[0]
    p.text = title
    p.font.size = Pt(28)
    p.font.bold = True
    p.font.color.rgb = COLOR_TEXT
    p.font.name = "Calibri"
    return slide

# ========== SLIDE 1: Title ==========
add_title_slide(prs,
    "AI Model Landscape April 2026: Benchmarking Intelligence, Speed, and Cost Across 11 Frontier Models",
    "Independent analysis from Artificial Analysis | April 2026")

# ========== SLIDE 2: Intelligence ==========
slide2 = add_content_slide(prs, "Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview and GPT-5.4 Co-Lead the Intelligence Index at 57")

# Table data
intel_data = [
    ("Rank", "Model", "Provider", "Index"),
    ("1", "Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview", "Google", "57"),
    ("2", "GPT-5.4 (xhigh)", "OpenAI", "57"),
    ("3", "Claude Opus 4.6 (max)", "Anthropic", "53"),
    ("4", "Muse Spark", "Meta", "52"),
    ("5", "Claude Sonnet 4.6 (max)", "Anthropic", "52"),
    ("6", "GLM-5.1", "Z AI", "51"),
    ("7", "Grok 4.20 0309 v2", "xAI", "49"),
    ("8", "Gemini 3 Flash", "Google", "46"),
    ("9", "DeepSeek V3.2", "DeepSeek", "42"),
    ("10", "NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Super", "NVIDIA", "36"),
    ("11", "gpt-oss-120B (high)", "OpenAI", "33"),
]

rows = len(intel_data)
cols = 4
left = Inches(0.6)
top = Inches(1.2)
width = Inches(8.5)
height = Inches(5.5)
table = slide2.shapes.add_table(rows, cols, left, top, width, height).table

# Column widths
table.columns[0].width = Inches(0.8)
table.columns[1].width = Inches(3.8)
table.columns[2].width = Inches(2.4)
table.columns[3].width = Inches(1.5)

for i, row in enumerate(intel_data):
    for j, val in enumerate(row):
        cell = table.cell(i, j)
        cell.text = val
        para = cell.text_frame.paragraphs[0]
        para.font.size = Pt(14)
        para.font.name = "Calibri"
        if i == 0:
            para.font.bold = True
            para.font.color.rgb = COLOR_TEXT
            cell.fill.solid()
            cell.fill.fore_color.rgb = RGBColor(30, 40, 60)
        else:
            para.font.color.rgb = COLOR_TEXT_DIM
            cell.fill.solid()
            cell.fill.fore_color.rgb = RGBColor(22, 30, 48)
        # Highlight top 2
        if i in (1, 2) and j == 3:
            para.font.bold = True
            para.font.color.rgb = COLOR_ACCENT

# Insight text on right
insight_box = slide2.shapes.add_textbox(Inches(9.4), Inches(1.2), Inches(3.3), Inches(5.5))
tf = insight_box.text_frame
tf.word_wrap = True
p = tf.paragraphs[0]
p.text = "Key Insight"
p.font.size = Pt(18)
p.font.bold = True
